01.r: The former commandment is put out of force.
01.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'a disannulling, setting aside' and cites this verse. He adds that in the Septuagint the word is usually used of unfaithful, rebellious action; here it is used of a rule being cancelled. The KJV's 'disannulling' is an old word for annulling.

02.r: Marks this statement as the first half of a contrast.
02.n: Abbott-Smith describes this particle as usually related to a following δέ or other adversative word, and calls it 'generally untranslatable'. Its partner does not fall within this verse. As in Hebrews 7:8, this study renders it 'on the one hand'.

03.r: Gives the reason or explanation for what has just been said about the new priest.

04.r: The setting aside happens; it is a present fact.
04.n: Present tense of the verb 'become, come about'. Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to come into being, arise'.

05.r: The commandment that came first, before the new priesthood.
05.n: A present participle, literally 'going before'. Abbott-Smith's first sense of the verb is 'to lead on, lead forth'; the brief's extract does not reach the intransitive sense used here, so 'going before' rests on the form and the context.

06.r: The command about priesthood, as in Hebrews 7:16.
06.n: Abbott-Smith cites Hebrews 7:16 and this verse together under the general sense 'a charge, injunction, order, command'.

07.r: Gives the reason for setting it aside.

08.r: Turns the two adjectives that follow into nouns: the weak and useless quality of it.
08.n: Literally 'the weak and unprofitable (thing) of it'. English needs nouns, 'weakness' and 'uselessness', so this word has no English of its own.

10.r: The commandment had no strength to do what was needed.
10.n: An adjective, 'weak', made into a noun by the article. Abbott-Smith builds it from a negative and σθένος, strength: 'without strength, weak, feeble', and cites this verse.

11.r: Joins the second fault to the first.

12.r: The commandment brought no real benefit.
12.n: Abbott-Smith builds it from a negative and ὄφελος, benefit, and gives 'unprofitable', and for the neuter used as a noun in this verse, 'unprofitableness'. 'Profit' here means benefit, not money.
